title: Enteric Pathogens in children under five with diarrhoea in a rotavirus vaccinated population in Coastal Ghana, 2023.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Despite the introduction and wide coverage of vaccination regimes such as rotavirus vaccination globally, diarrhoea remains a major public health problem with new studies showing an emerging pattern in its etiology.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a cross-sectional study of children under five years reporting with diarrhoea at the district health facility in the Anloga district, Ghana.
analysis.methods: Stool samples of diarrhoea cases were tested for pathogens and co-infections using standard ELISA methods and TAQMAN Array Card RT-PCR Technology. The Vesikari Clinical Severity Scoring System was used to classify diarrhoea severity. Data generated was described descriptively.
analysis.main_results: The Rotavirus A prevalence was 2.5%. The pathogen with the highest prevalence was Enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC) (52.6%, 20/38), Shigella/Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (Shigella/EIEC (76.3%, 29/38), Norovirus (26.3%, 10/38) and Giardia was the main parasite identified. The rate of co-infection was high (94.7%, 36/38). Co-infections with bacteria-virus present had more moderate-severe diarrhoea cases (73.3%, 11/15). Norovirus was present in most of the severe cases (75%, 3/4).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The leading diarrhoea pathogens found were EAEC, Shigella/EIEC and Norovirus. The rate of pathogen co-infection was very high with bacteria-virus related co-infections affecting diarrhoea severity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study recommends periodic diarrhoea pathogen surveillance through Ghana Health Service collaborating with research institutions such as Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research (NMIMR). Also, enhancing water, sanitation and hygiene practices at the district, community and individual levels as a means of diarrhoea prevention in the absence of additional vaccines for other diarrhoea pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report on design limitations, bias, confounding, sample size, controls, generalisability, or abstract-only evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the etiology of diarrhoea in children under five years in a rotavirus vaccinated population in Coastal Ghana. The research aimed to identify the leading pathogens causing diarrhoea and assess the impact of co-infections. Stool samples were tested using ELISA and RT-PCR methods, revealing that Norovirus had a prevalence of 26.3%, while Enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC) and Shigella/EIEC were the most common pathogens. Co-infections were prevalent, with 94.7% of cases involving multiple pathogens, and these co-infections were associated with more severe diarrhoea. The findings highlight the need for targeted surveillance and improved hygiene practices to address diarrhoea in the absence of vaccines for other pathogens. The study's results are descriptive and do not provide detailed statistical analysis, which may limit the confidence in the conclusions.

title: Viral gastroenteritis: Molecular epidemiology of human norovirus by RT-PCR at University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of Congo

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a major public health concern in Africa, with noroviruses recognized as predominant viral etiological agents. However, their epidemiological impact remains underreported in the Republic of Congo, particularly in Brazzaville.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from June to November 2020 at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville. Fifty children aged 28 days to 17 years presenting with AGE were enrolled, with eighty percent aged ≤5 years.
analysis.methods: Stool samples were analyzed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect viral RNA and differentiate between GI and GII genogroups.
analysis.main_results: The overall prevalence of norovirus infection was 44%, with GII (73%) predominating over GI (18%). GI/GII co-infections were detected in 9% of cases. A significant association was observed between age and norovirus genogroup distribution (p = 0.03), with GII being more prevalent among children aged ≤5 years.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Norovirus represents an important cause of pediatric AGE in Brazzaville. The study identified GII as the dominant genogroup and highlighted age-related differences in genogroup distribution.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the integration of molecular diagnostic approaches into national surveillance programs and the strengthening of sanitation measures to improve prevention and control strategies for norovirus gastroenteritis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s cross-sectional design and small sample size limit causal inference and generalizability. The evidence strength is assessed as moderate due to potential selection bias and lack of longitudinal follow-up.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the molecular epidemiology of human norovirus among children with acute gastroenteritis (AGE) in Brazzaville, Republic of Congo. Conducted from June to November 2020 at the University Hospital Center, it enrolled 50 children aged 28 days to 17 years, with 80% aged ≤5 years. Using real-time RT-PCR, the overall norovirus prevalence was 44%, with GII (73%) predominating over GI (18%) and 9% exhibiting GI/GII co-infections. A significant age association was found (p = 0.03), with GII more prevalent in children ≤5 years. Clinical manifestations did not differ significantly between genogroups (p > 0.05). The study concludes norovirus is a key cause of pediatric AGE locally and recommends integrating molecular diagnostics into surveillance and improving sanitation. Limitations include the small sample size, cross-sectional design, and potential selection bias, warranting cautious interpretation.

title: Treatment With Ruxolitinib and TAK-779 Enhances GII.17 Human Norovirus Replication and Enables Serial Passaging in Human Intestinal Enteroids.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human norovirus (HuNoV) is a major cause of acute viral gastroenteritis. Although it can be replicated in vitro using human intestinal enteroids (HIEs), generating high-titer viral laboratory stocks remains challenging due to low infection and passage efficiencies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we evaluated the effect of their inhibitors, ruxolitinib-a Janus kinase (JAK) 1/JAK2 inhibitor-and TAK-779-a C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3)/C-C motif chemokine receptor (CCR) 5/CCR2 antagonist-on HuNoV replication in wild-type jejunal HIEs.
analysis.methods: Interferon response and chemokine signaling may be key host pathways that restrict efficient HuNoV replication.
analysis.main_results: TAK-779 increased GII.17 HuNoV replication by 2.3- and 6.0-fold at 48 and 96 h postinfection (hpi), respectively, compared with the DMSO-treated control.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: In contrast, ruxolitinib alone did not affect viral replication.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Notably, simultaneous treatment with these compounds further enhanced GII.17 replication by 6.0- and 10.7-fold at 48 and 96 hpi, respectively, which enabled serial passaging.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: These findings imply that the simultaneous suppression of these pathways potentially benefits GII.17 HuNoV replication.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of ruxolitinib and TAK-779 on GII.17 human norovirus (HuNoV) replication in human intestinal enteroids (HIEs). The research aimed to address the challenge of generating high-titer viral stocks due to low replication efficiency. The results showed that TAK-779 significantly increased viral replication at 48 and 96 hpi, while ruxolitinib alone had no effect. Simultaneous treatment with both compounds led to a further enhancement, enabling serial passaging. These findings suggest that targeting interferon response and chemokine signaling pathways could improve HuNoV replication in vitro. The study provides insights into potential therapeutic strategies for norovirus infections but has limited implications for broader applications due to its focus on a specific viral genotype and in vitro model.

title: Zymosan-adjuvanted intranasal norovirus virus-like particle vaccine induces antiviral mucosal immune responses in infant mice.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenge of developing pain-free mucosal vaccines for infants, as their immune systems are less mature and injectable vaccines cause discomfort. There is an urgent need for vaccines optimized for immunologically immature infants.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used an infant murine model to examine the effectiveness of an intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle (VLP) vaccine with zymosan as an adjuvant. The vaccine was tested in infant mice to assess its ability to induce immune responses.
analysis.methods: The researchers administered the intranasal zymosan-adjuvanted VLP vaccine to infant mice and compared the resulting immune responses to those induced by VLPs alone. They measured levels of intestinal and salivary VLP-specific IgA antibodies and plasma VLP-specific IgG antibodies.
analysis.main_results: Infant mice given a minimum dose of the zymosan-adjuvanted VLP vaccine showed increased levels of intestinal and salivary VLP-specific IgA antibodies, as well as plasma VLP-specific IgG antibodies, comparable to those in adults. In contrast, infant mice receiving VLPs alone had substantially weaker immune responses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the zymosan-adjuvanted norovirus VLP vaccine can effectively induce mucosal immune responses in infants, which is a novel approach for developing vaccines tailored to their immunological needs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide important insights into the development of mucosal vaccines for infants, which could reduce the need for painful injections and improve the efficiency of achieving protective immunity against norovirus.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to an infant murine model, which may not fully represent human immune responses. However, the evidence is strong as it directly compares vaccine-induced immune responses in infants to those in adults using a well-defined experimental setup.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the potential of a zymosan-adjuvanted intranasal norovirus virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine to induce mucosal immune responses in infant mice. The research was motivated by the need for pain-free vaccines for infants, as injectable vaccines are less effective and cause discomfort. Using an infant murine model, the study found that the zymosan-adjuvanted VLP vaccine significantly increased levels of intestinal and salivary VLP-specific IgA antibodies and plasma VLP-specific IgG antibodies in infant mice, comparable to those in adults. These findings suggest that the vaccine could be an effective mucosal vaccine candidate for infants, potentially reducing the need for multiple painful injections. The study's results are relevant for developing vaccines optimized for immunologically immature hosts, but its reliance on a murine model limits direct applicability to humans.

title: Detection of Norovirus in Children 0-5 Years Presenting with Acute Diarrhoea in Three Selected Tertiary Health Facilities in Jos, Plateau State, Nigeria

analysis.research_question_and_background: Norovirus is a global health concern and is considered a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis across all age groups, resulting in sporadic infections and epidemic or endemic outbreaks worldwide. Human norovirus infection accounts for substantial morbidity and mortality annually, particularly among children younger than 5 years.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among paediatric inpatients and general outpatient attendees from January to November 2020. Consenting participants were recruited using simple random sampling, and a stool sample was collected from each child.
analysis.methods: Data were analysed using STATA statistical software, version 15. Norovirus antigen was detected in 61 of 184 samples using the MyBioSource Norovirus Antigen enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, giving an overall prevalence of 33.2%.
analysis.main_results: Norovirus was detected throughout the study period, with the highest monthly proportion recorded in March (34.4%). Plateau State Specialist Hospital accounted for the largest proportion of positive cases (68.9%), and the difference by facility was statistically significant.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The observed prevalence highlights the need to strengthen norovirus prevention, surveillance, and control interventions in Jos and to support evidence-informed consideration of future vaccination strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the importance of targeted norovirus surveillance and prevention strategies in children under five in Jos, particularly in tertiary health facilities, to mitigate the burden of acute gastroenteritis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, which cannot establish causality, and the potential for sampling bias. The evidence is moderate as it provides prevalence data but lacks longitudinal or interventional components.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the prevalence of norovirus among children aged 0-5 years with acute diarrhoea in three tertiary health facilities in Jos, Nigeria. Using a descriptive cross-sectional design, stool samples were collected from 184 participants between January and November 2020, and norovirus antigen was detected in 61 samples (33.2%). The highest proportion of positive cases was observed at Plateau State Specialist Hospital (68.9%), with a statistically significant difference across facilities. Norovirus infections peaked in March (34.4%) and were most common in children aged 7–12 months (32.8%). Although sex was not significantly associated with infection, body temperature showed a significant link, with 45.9% of positive cases occurring in children with temperatures of 38.0–38.9°C. The study highlights the need for improved prevention, surveillance, and control measures in Jos, emphasizing the importance of hygiene practices to reduce norovirus transmission. The evidence is moderate due to the cross-sectional design and lack of interventional data.

title: Wastewater and Environmental Surveillance in Cities with Sewered and Non-sewered Sanitation: Evidence from Kampala, Uganda

analysis.research_question_and_background: Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) enables community-level monitoring of infectious diseases. Most progress has focused on sewer-based surveillance, yet nearly half of the global population relies on non-sewered sanitation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Ten drainage channel sampling points with delineated micro-catchments (0.95-3.83 km2 with 12,885-44,146 people) were selected within Kampala. A total of 255 drainage channel and 54 wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) influent samples were collected during two campaigns in March and September-October 2025.
analysis.methods: A multi-target panel was quantified by digital PCR, including enteric viruses (Norovirus GI and GII, Rotavirus), respiratory viruses (SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and B viruses, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)), non-O1/O139 Vibrio cholerae (V. cholerae), and Pepper Mild Mottle Virus (PMMoV) as a fecal indicator.
analysis.main_results: Enteric viruses, non-O1/O139 V. cholerae, and PMMoV were consistently detected across all drainage channels and WWTP influents. Concentrations were generally lower in drainage than WWTP influents, except for non-O1/O139 V. When normalized by PMMoV, concentrations across most drainage channels were comparable to WWTP influents, although comparability varied by target and location.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: PMMoV-normalized concentrations across most micro-catchments were comparable to WWTP influents, with spatial heterogeneity implying neighborhood-level differences in disease prevalence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Catchment-delineated drainage surveillance has potential to offer spatially resolved public health information in non-sewered settings comparable to sewer-based wastewater monitoring.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Trends between campaigns varied by pathogen target and were not explained by any single micro-catchment characteristic. The evidence strength is moderate due to the variability in results and the lack of detailed explanations for observed trends.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the potential of wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) in non-sewered urban settings, specifically focusing on Kampala, Uganda. It evaluates the detection of enteric and respiratory viruses, including Norovirus GI and GII, Rotavirus, and SARS-CoV-2, in urban drainage channels and wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) influents. The study collected 255 drainage channel and 54 WWTP influent samples during two campaigns in 2025. Using digital PCR, the researchers quantified a multi-target panel, including Norovirus GI and GII, Rotavirus, and PMMoV as a fecal indicator. The results showed consistent detection of enteric viruses and PMMoV across all sampling points, with lower concentrations in drainage channels compared to WWTP influents, except for non-O1/O139 V. cholerae. When normalized by PMMoV, concentrations in most drainage channels were comparable to WWTP influents, though this varied by location and target. The study highlights the potential of drainage-based WES to provide spatially resolved public health data in non-sewered areas, similar to sewer-based monitoring. However, the findings are limited by the variability in trends between campaigns and the lack of clear explanations for these variations. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations and the absence of detailed causal interpretations.

title: Microbial assessment of recontamination with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter in patient room environment in a burn unit.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Healthcare-associated transmission of pathogens is influenced by environmental persistence and recontamination, yet the rapidity of recontamination with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii after disinfection in high-risk units remains insufficiently characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This prospective environmental sampling study was conducted in a burn intensive care unit to quantify the time to recontamination of surfaces with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii after terminal disinfection.
analysis.methods: Six high-touch environmental sites were sampled using Rodac plates at 1-hour intervals for 10 hours following standard disinfection procedures.
analysis.main_results: Recontamination with Acinetobacter occurred rapidly: overbed table and IV pump at 2 hours, and chair and stock cabinet at 3 hours.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that recontamination occurs within hours after cleaning, highlighting the inadequacy of conventional disinfection and the need for continuous or enhanced environmental cleaning strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the implementation of continuous disinfection methods in burn units to reduce healthcare-associated transmission of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to a single burn unit, a short observation window, and did not assess transmission to patients, warranting cautious interpretation and larger-scale validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the rapidity of environmental recontamination with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii in a burn intensive care unit after disinfection. Six high-touch surfaces were sampled hourly for 10 hours using Rodac plates. Recontamination occurred within 2–3 hours on all sampled sites, demonstrating that surfaces become recontaminated quickly even after cleaning. The authors interpreted these results as evidence that conventional disinfection is insufficient and that continuous or enhanced environmental cleaning is necessary to prevent transmission. The findings imply that burn units should adopt continuous disinfection strategies to reduce healthcare-associated Acinetobacter transmission. However, the study’s single-centre design, short follow-up, and lack of patient outcome data limit generalisability and strength of evidence.

title: Detection Patterns and Temporal Dynamics of Multiple Pathogens in Wastewater Using a TaqMan Array Card

analysis.research_question_and_background: Wastewater-based surveillance (WBS) complements clinical surveillance by capturing community-level circulation of infectious diseases, including asymptomatic infections. However, most multipathogen WBS studies have focused on pathogen detection and detection frequency, with limited evaluation of temporal changes using semi-quantitative Ct values.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Weekly influent samples (500 mL) were collected from two wastewater treatment plants in Cheonan and Asan during weeks 21~52 of 2025 (64 total samples). The TAC targeted 31 pathogen analysis groups encompassing respiratory, enteric, and selected high-concern pathogens, along with seven antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs).
analysis.methods: Pathogen occurrence was evaluated based on week-based detection status and detection frequency, while Ct values were interpreted as a semi-quantitative indicator for exploratory assessment of temporal changes. Samples failing the predefined quality control criteria were re-extracted and reanalyzed, and all samples were ultimately included in the final analysis.
analysis.main_results: Ten pathogens, including SARS-CoV-2, norovirus, adenovirus type F, and human rhinovirus, were detected in 100% of the study weeks. Semi-quantitative Ct values showed no consistent increasing or decreasing trend for SARS-CoV-2, but they declined during winter for norovirus and influenza A.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrated that norovirus detection patterns in wastewater can be characterized using a TaqMan Array Card, and that semi-quantitative Ct values can provide insights into temporal changes in viral load.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the use of TAC-based WBS as an integrated tool for community-level infectious disease surveillance, particularly for tracking norovirus and other pathogens with seasonal variations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not include specific analysis of norovirus subtypes or genogroups, and the semi-quantitative nature of Ct values may limit the precision of temporal trend assessments. Confidence in the findings is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to characterize multipathogen detection patterns in wastewater using a TaqMan Array Card (TAC) and explore temporal changes using semi-quantitative Ct values. Weekly influent samples were collected from two wastewater treatment plants in Cheonan and Asan during weeks 21~52 of 2025, targeting 31 pathogens and seven antimicrobial resistance genes. The results showed that norovirus was detected in all study weeks, with semi-quantitative Ct values declining during winter. The findings support TAC-based wastewater-based surveillance as a tool for community-level infectious disease monitoring, particularly for tracking norovirus and other pathogens with seasonal variations. However, the study's limitations include the lack of subtype-specific analysis and the potential imprecision of Ct values in assessing temporal trends, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

title: Evolution, diversity and distribution of human Noroviruses:From single hosts to global patterns

analysis.research_question_and_background: Norovirus causes substantial global morbidity and mortality from acute gastroenteritis, yet key knowledge gaps persist regarding its high diversity, within-host and community-level evolution, and links between diversity and treatment outcomes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This thesis synthesizes existing evidence to address norovirus diversity and epidemiology across hosts and populations, integrating host-specific analyses and wastewater-based sequencing for population-level monitoring.
analysis.methods: The study employs a comparative and integrative approach, combining literature review with wastewater-based sequencing to examine viral diversity and circulation patterns at the population level.
analysis.main_results: The thesis identifies over 10 genogroups (GI–GX) and approximately 50 genotypes, with GII.4 continuously generating new antigenic variants, highlighting the virus's extensive diversity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The work interprets the observed diversity as a driver of therapeutic challenges and proposes wastewater-based sequencing as a tool to monitor norovirus evolution and circulation, emphasizing the need to bridge within-host and community-level evolutionary insights.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform surveillance strategies and underscore the urgency for vaccine and antiviral development, given the absence of licensed options and the virus's antigenic variability.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by its reliance on a literature-based synthesis and wastewater sequencing, which may not capture all host-specific dynamics or treatment associations, warranting moderate confidence in the conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This thesis examines norovirus diversity and epidemiology to address critical gaps in understanding its evolution and public health impact. It synthesizes evidence showing norovirus as a major global cause of acute gastroenteritis, with over 10 genogroups and 50 genotypes, including the antigenically variable GII.4. The study integrates host-specific analyses and wastewater-based sequencing to monitor viral diversity and circulation at the population level. Key findings highlight the virus's extensive diversity as a barrier to therapeutic and vaccine development, with no licensed antivirals or vaccines currently available. The work interprets these patterns as evidence of ongoing antigenic drift and calls for improved surveillance and intervention strategies. Limitations include the reliance on literature synthesis and wastewater data, which may not fully capture host-specific dynamics or treatment outcomes, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

title: Colorimetric-Catalytic-SERS Trimodal Immunochromatographic Assay for Multi-Scenario Monitoring of Gastrointestinal Infections.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the persistent technical challenges in directly detecting pathogens in stool samples, which is the gold standard for diagnosing gastrointestinal infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors developed a versatile immunochromatographic assay (ICA) integrating magnetic enrichment with colorimetric, catalytic, and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) signals for simultaneous detection of bacteria and viruses.
analysis.methods: A self-assembled magnetic SERS nanozyme was created by layer-by-layer deposition of PtIr nanoparticles and Au nanostars onto a magnetic core to provide peroxidase-like activity and electromagnetic enhancement. A multi-feature fusion neural-network model was designed for intelligent SERS signal analysis to quantify pathogen concentrations.
analysis.main_results: In colorimetric mode, visual limits of detection (vLODs) were 5 × 103 CFU/mL for Escherichia coli O157 and 0.05 ng/mL for norovirus. In catalytic mode, a 2 min substrate-catalysis step reduced the colorimetric vLOD by 100-fold. In SERS mode, detection limits were further lowered to 8 CFU/mL and 0.11 pg/mL via a quantitative algorithm.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Application to 116 clinical stool samples showed detection rates consistent with quantitative real-time PCR while reducing assay time to 1/8, demonstrating the method's potential for rapid and accurate detection of gastrointestinal infections.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This trimodal ICA offers a promising approach for rapid, accurate, and multi-scenario monitoring of gastrointestinal infections, potentially improving diagnostic workflows in clinical settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's clinical validation was limited to 116 stool samples and did not include a direct comparison of norovirus detection performance against other established assays beyond consistency with qPCR, which may affect generalisability.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a trimodal immunochromatographic assay (ICA) combining magnetic enrichment with colorimetric, catalytic, and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) signals for detecting gastrointestinal pathogens, including norovirus. The assay employs a magnetic SERS nanozyme with peroxidase-like activity and a neural-network model for SERS signal analysis. In clinical validation with 116 stool samples, the method achieved detection limits of 0.11 pg/mL for norovirus and reduced assay time to one-eighth of conventional methods while maintaining consistency with quantitative real-time PCR. The approach demonstrates potential for rapid, accurate, and multi-scenario monitoring of gastrointestinal infections, though validation was limited in sample size and comparative scope.

title: Simplified Linear Dose‐Response Models for Low‐Dose QMRAs

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study analyzes widely used dose‐response (DR) models from potable reuse quantitative microbial risk assessments (QMRAs) to identify the low‐dose ranges where the log 10 ‐transformed probability of infection and pathogen dose exhibit a linear relationship.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examines dose-response models for human noroviruses, including norovirus, Norwalk virus, norovirus infection, norovirus gastroenteritis, Norovirus GI, Norovirus GII, GII.4 norovirus, norovirus GII.4, and norovirus gastroenteritis, to assess their behavior in low-dose ranges relevant to potable reuse.
analysis.methods: This study defines the low‐dose linear range for each DR model, extracts slope and intercept parameters via regression, and shows that municipal drinking water risk thresholds fall within these ranges.
analysis.main_results: This study shows that within the low‐dose ranges relevant to potable reuse, commonly used DR models exhibit linear relationships with a slope of ~1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Therefore, each 10‐fold reduction in pathogen concentration, equivalent to one log reduction value (LRV), reduces risk by a corresponding order of magnitude.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This promotes low‐dose risk estimation transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility for utility decision making, regardless of the underlying complexity of the DR model.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Finally, the outputs from the various DR models are separated by relatively constant risk differentials, thereby reducing the need for complex DR‐based sensitivity analyses when conducting potable reuse QMRAs.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates dose-response (DR) models used in potable reuse quantitative microbial risk assessments (QMRAs) to identify low-dose ranges where the relationship between log 10 -transformed probability of infection and pathogen dose is linear. The research focuses on human noroviruses, including Norovirus GI and GII, and their relevance to water safety. The study defines the low-dose linear range for each DR model, extracts slope and intercept parameters via regression, and demonstrates that municipal drinking water risk thresholds fall within these ranges. It finds that within these low-dose ranges, commonly used DR models exhibit linear relationships with a slope of ~1, meaning each 10-fold reduction in pathogen concentration reduces risk by an order of magnitude. The results suggest that the outputs from different DR models differ by relatively constant risk values, reducing the need for complex sensitivity analyses. The study's findings promote transparency and reproducibility in low-dose risk estimation for utility decision-making. However, the study does not provide detailed limitations or evidence strength assessments.
